syllabus.clause: reading n, value ranges and time limits as a budget

at.step: A statement says n is at most a hundred thousand and the time limit is one second. The obvious double loop over every pair costs ten billion steps, about a hundred seconds on an ordinary machine. The limit has already answered the question, before the problem itself is even understood.

The starting point for every such estimate is one fact: an ordinary modern machine performs on the order of a hundred million simple operations in a second. A time limit, multiplied by that rate, turns into a budget of operations — a number to compare an algorithm against before writing a line of it.

syllabus.clause: (n ≤ 20 → 2ⁿ; n ≤ 10⁵ → n log n; n ≤ 10⁸ → linear, cache-friendly)

at.step: That single division, repeated for every growth rate, is the whole table: n at ten allows a factorial amount of work; twenty allows two to the n; five hundred allows n cubed; five thousand allows n squared; a million allows n log n or better; and once n is large, only constant or logarithmic work fits. Nothing here is memorised — every row falls out of the same division.

The rule of thumb's hundred million operations a second quietly assumed every operation hits the cache. Near the top of the budget, around a hundred million elements, the work has to be one sequential pass — because a random access per element is a cache miss, and that assumption breaks. Measured directly: the same count of reads, done once in order and once in random order, and the random pass runs reliably slower.

A smaller input size does not just forbid algorithms, it can permit ones that were hopeless at a larger size. At n of forty, trying two to the n choices outright costs well over a trillion operations. Splitting the forty choices into two halves of twenty, and combining the two results, costs only two to the twenty per half — a few million, not a trillion.

Predict: when an exact algorithm still fails to fit the budget, even at a small input size, and the input size looks deliberately kept small, is that only a statement about speed — or can it also be a signal about the problem itself?

A budget only ever rules algorithms out. Fitting inside it is a necessary condition, never a sufficient one — an algorithm that fits the budget can still be the wrong algorithm, computing the wrong answer quickly.

Four words in a statement each hint at a technique, each checked here against a brute force on a small case: "sorted" points at binary search; "k-th" points at a heap; "all pairs" asks whether n squared is even affordable; "minimum maximum" points at binary search over the answer itself, a monotone predicate.

items.item: The 'minimum maximum' signal's binary-search-on-the-answer technique requires the predicate 'is there a solution with maximum at most x' to be monotone in x (true for all x above some threshold, false below it) — this topic's own examples.py verifies this for the specific split-into-k-pieces predicate it builds, by brute force on small instances, rather than asserting monotonicity holds for every problem that superficially resembles a 'minimum maximum' statement.

items.item: 'Necessary, never sufficient' describes the budget's logical relationship to correctness precisely: an algorithm fitting the budget tells you nothing about whether it computes the right answer, and an algorithm failing the budget is ruled out regardless of whether it would have been correct — the topic's own three-question routine at the close is explicitly a filter, not a design procedure that produces a correct algorithm by itself.

Complexity budgeting is the cheapest of the chapter's four reading skills specifically because it is checkable from the statement alone, before the problem's actual content (what it is asking, what structure fits it) is understood at all — the topic's own ordering (budget first, structure second, graph third, reduction fourth) mirrors the cost of applying each check, not an arbitrary syllabus sequence.
